Adult Atlantic menhaden commonly attain a maximum recorded total length of 50 centimeters [Li = 50 centimeters], a size seldom exceeded even among the oldest individuals within a population. Field surveys of spawning aggregations along the mid-Atlantic coast indicate that the onset of reproductive maturity is closely tied to body size, with puberty typically occurring once fish reach approximately 25 centimeters [Lp = approximately 25 centimeters] in total length. This length-based threshold ensures that individuals have amassed sufficient somatic mass before investing in gonadal development. The energetic implications of this size-based maturation schedule are substantial; pubertal individuals have a corresponding wet body mass of roughly 215.6 grams [Wwp = roughly 215.6 grams], marking a significant increase over the mass carried at earlier life stages. Data collected from extensive seine-net samples suggest that fully grown, asymptotic adults can achieve a maximum wet weight of 1848 grams [Wwi = 1848 grams], a value consistent with the species' relatively rapid early growth trajectory, which slows considerably after sexual maturation is attained. This ultimate body mass places the species among the larger members of the Clupeidae family in the western North Atlantic.

The initial life stages of Atlantic menhaden involve a remarkably small mass at the point of yolk-sac resorption. Following eclosion, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves, carries a wet weight at birth of only 0.00045 grams [Wwb = 0.00045 grams]. This extremely low neonatal mass reflects the tiny egg diameter, approximately 0.95 millimeters, documented in the closely related Gulf menhaden Brevoortia patronus. The period between fertilization and the hatching event itself is brief but strongly temperature-dependent. When incubation proceeds at a stable water temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C], the age at birth from fertilization is approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days]. This developmental rate is consistent with the thermal regime typical of the species' primary winter-spring spawning grounds, where cool shelf waters slow embryonic metabolism and prolong the pre-hatching interval compared to more southerly clupeid populations.

Under the same thermal conditions of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C], the species exhibits a remarkable maximum reproductive output when viewed on an annual scale. A single reproductively active female of Atlantic menhaden can release approximately 631,000 eggs over the course of a single spawning season [Ri = approximately 631,000 eggs over the course of a single spawning season]. This immense fecundity per season, characteristic of a highly fecund broadcast spawner, compensates for the high mortality rates experienced during the early planktonic larval phase. When considered alongside the observation that females typically participate in just one major spawning pulse each year [F_R_i = one major spawning pulse each year], the annual reproductive investment becomes clear: a single female can direct well over half a million oocytes into the water column annually. This strategy of releasing very high numbers of small, low-cost oocytes is typical of pelagic spawners in productive coastal upwelling and estuarine systems, where food for larvae is seasonally abundant but highly unpredictable in its spatial distribution.

Longevity records for Atlantic menhaden, derived from otolith-based age estimates collected during routine NOAA fisheries monitoring cruises, indicate a maximum documented lifespan of 7 years [am = 7 years] at a temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C]. This relatively extended lifespan for a fast-growing, highly fecund clupeid is maintained under the cool thermal conditions (13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C]) characteristic of the northern portion of its range, where reduced metabolic rates may slow the accumulation of cellular damage. In contrast, individuals from warmer southern populations may experience somewhat earlier senescence, although precise comparative data remain limited. The combination of a moderate lifespan, a large ultimate body size, and an exceptionally high annual fecundity places the species firmly within an opportunistic life-history strategy, adapted to exploit pulsed blooms of phytoplankton and zooplankton in estuaries and coastal waters. This strategy is particularly effective given the species' role as a filter feeder, linking primary and secondary production to higher trophic levels.

The seasonal migration patterns of Atlantic menhaden are tightly linked to thermal cues, with large schools moving northward along the Atlantic coast of the United States as spring surface waters warm. During the winter months, the fish aggregate in deeper, warmer offshore waters off North Carolina, where the prevailing temperature of approximately 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C] supports continued low-level metabolic function. The species' growth rate is notably rapid during the first two years of life, with juveniles often exceeding 20 centimeters in fork length by the end of their first growing season. This rapid early growth, coupled with a maximum longevity of 7 years [am = 7 years], suggests that individuals experience a narrow window of peak reproductive contribution, typically between ages three and five, before the onset of gradual physiological decline at a temperature of 13.2 °C [T = 13.2 °C]. The population structure observed in commercial catch data frequently reflects this pattern, with a strong mode of 3- to 5-year-old fish dominating the spawning stock biomass. Continued monitoring of age-frequency distributions is critical for sustaining the fishery, which is one of the largest by volume on the U.S. East Coast.
